verses.1:
Al-Mizan reads takwīr as the sun's circular wrapping, perhaps metaphorically in darkness. Inkidār describes the stars' disintegration and fall, though it may mean their loss of light; mountains move in the Hour's quake and become dust and mirage. The abandonment of the precious pregnant camels is a metaphor for the Day's self-preoccupation, when even most valued possessions are left unclaimed.

The commentary apparently takes the mustering of wild beasts as their resurrection with humanity, supported by (6:38), while their later fate is neither stated in the Qur'an nor reliably narrated; it allows the less likely reading that they leave their dens before the Resurrection. Tasjīr of the seas may mean setting them ablaze or filling them until they overflow. Souls are coupled: the happy with heavenly spouses and the wretched with devils as enduring companions.

Al-Mizan explains mawʾūdah as a girl buried alive, an Arab custom motivated by fear of disgrace. Questioning her about the sin for which she was killed censures the father, enables her grievance against him, and prepares his punishment. It also allows the figurative reading that she is asked about, meaning that the murderer is questioned concerning her.

verses.10: Al-Mizan says the records of deeds are unfolded for reckoning; the sky is stripped off by the tearing apart of what is tightly bound, that is, its rolling up. Hell is stirred until aflame, and paradise is brought close to its inhabitants. These events complete the repeated ‘when’: every soul, meaning all people, will know the acts it has made present for itself, as in (3:30).

verses.15: Al-Mizan interprets al-khunnas, al-jawārī, and al-kunnas as heavenly bodies that retreat, move rapidly, and hide, most plausibly the five planets Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury. Their observed prograde motion (istiqāmah), retrograde motion (rajʿah), and apparent station (iqāmah) respectively fit movement, retreat, and an animal's withdrawal to its lair. It considers all heavenly bodies, which disappear by day, move by night, and hide at setting, a less convincing interpretation; reading the terms as buffaloes or deer, illustrative of wild animals, is still less apparent.

verses.17: Al-Mizan notes that ʿasʿasah can mean both the night's advance and retreat, including the dimness of twilight and dawn. In light of the following dawn, it prefers the end of night to the alternative beginning-of-night reading.
verses.18: Al-Mizan treats the dawn's ‘breathing’ as a metaphor for light spreading across the horizons and removing the darkness that allows rest after the day's labor. It reports al-Zamakhsharī's alternative that the figure refers to the refreshing morning breeze, but finds the spreading light the more immediate meaning.
verses.19: Al-Mizan takes ‘it’ to mean the whole Qur'an, or these verses as part of it, and identifies the noble messenger as Gabriel through (2:97). Calling it Gabriel's speech attributes it to him as the message-bearer, while it remains God's speech. Gabriel is God's messenger, noble, powerful, eminent in rank with the Lord of the Throne, obeyed in the divine realm and thus commanding angelic assistants, and trustworthy, conveying revelation without distortion or treachery. The commentary rejects identifying this messenger as the Prophet because the following verses do not support it.

verses.22: Al-Mizan says ‘your companion’ refutes the allegation that the Prophet is insane: his hearers have lived among him and know his sound judgment, reliable views, and truthful speech. Gabriel's detailed praise does not imply Gabriel's superiority, because the argument is establishing a faultless channel of revelation rather than enumerating the receiver's qualities; clearing the Prophet of madness is sufficient to that purpose. The commentary adds that the Qur'an's other descriptions of the Prophet leave no doubt that he is superior to all angels, who were made to prostrate before the human being as God's vicegerent on earth.
verses.23: Al-Mizan identifies the Prophet as the one who saw Gabriel on the manifest horizon, apparently the elevated horizon of the angelic world also meant in (53:7). It rejects locating the sight in the eastern sunrise or insisting that Gabriel appeared in his original form: narrations of his throne between heaven and earth should be understood as tamaththul, appearance or representation. The Prophet is not ḍanīn—one firmly disposed to miserliness—with respect to the Unseen revealed to him; he neither conceals, withholds, nor alters any of it, but teaches it as God commanded.

verses.25: Al-Mizan rejects the claim that the Qur'an is Satanic communication, a charge broader than the allegation of insanity. Shayṭān originally means a malicious being and can include not only Iblīs and his progeny but other mischievous jinn; rajīm, outcast, is likewise not exclusive to Iblīs. The Qur'an is therefore neither Iblīs's temptation nor an inspiration of jinn thought to possess the insane.
verses.26: Al-Mizan says the preceding verses establish that the Qur'an is God's word; Gabriel, its high-ranking and trustworthy angelic bearer, receives, preserves, and conveys it without impediment; the familiar Prophet received it, is not insane, and neither withholds nor changes it; and it is not communication from Iblīs or mischievous jinn. These points prepare the conclusion that it guides whoever seeks truth. ‘So where are you going?’ is therefore a rhetorical rebuke: given these facts, why turn away and call the Qur'an insanity or a Satanic message?
verses.27: Al-Mizan calls the Qur'an a reminder and admonition for all peoples, but says its benefit is actualized for those who will to remain steadfast in truth through servitude and obedience. It then answers the misconception that this makes people independent in volition or makes God dependent on their steadfastness: they cannot will steadfastness unless God wills that they will it. Voluntary human acts are thus themselves willed by God, who wills each person to act in a particular way through that person's own volition.
